work_packages.name: An agent writes a game's scenes, phases and rules in plain Rust against one crate, in the order they run, and proves them in an ordinary test with no window
work_packages.quality_bar: Game code that reads as plainly as Bevy's `breakout` example with less ceremony: a scene function reads top to bottom as one tick, and no line names engine plumbing. Compiler and startup messages as useful as Rust's own, each naming the object, the cause and the next step. Correctness held as `SIM-2D` holds it: one trace, one digest. The reference for how game code reads is the design's worked examples, which the owner approves.

items.statement: Written order, and what a rule sees, in a game with no window built from `thrum` alone and stepped through `game.test()`. Build this item first: it rests on the engine applying a rule's structural edits when the rule ends, inside the tick's one transaction. (1) The entries of a scene function run once a tick in the order written, across `scene.rules` blocks and `scene.phase` blocks, and a phase block's rules run only while that is the scene's phase. (2) A rule reads what earlier rules of the same tick wrote to components and resources. (3) An entity a rule spawns is visited by no query of that rule and by the queries of every later rule of the same tick. An entity a rule despawns is still visited for the rest of that rule and by no later rule. A component inserted or removed is seen from the next rule on. (4) `despawn` returns true for the call that despawns an entity, and false for a second call in the same rule and for any later call. (5) A query visits entities in the order they were spawned, on every run, and its `With` and `Without` filters select as written. `Single` gives the one match, and refuses the tick with none and with two. (6) An event a rule sends is read by later rules of that tick and by none in the next. (7) `rule.every(d)` runs first at the end of the first interval after its phase or scene was entered and once each interval after, and a rule or group under `when` runs only in ticks where its condition holds. (8) `par_each` leaves the world as the serial loop does. (9) A component is known to the world, with no list written by the game, when the signature of a listed function names it, and a component that only a spawned tuple holds is known once the game says `Game::component::<T>()`. Guard: CPU tests on worlds of a few entities, in `./dev check`.

Scenes, phases and time, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. (1) The game starts in the first scene listed, with its default value, and `test_in` starts in a given one. (2) A change of scene lands when the tick ends, in this order: the phase's exit functions, the scene's exit functions, the scene's entities despawned, scene resources set to the values they were registered with, the new scene's enter functions in the order written, the first phase's enter functions. Game resources keep their values. The next tick's first rule sees all of it, and reads the scene's value as `Res<S>` with the fields it was entered with. `restart()` enters the running scene again with the same value. (3) A change of phase lands when the tick ends, the old phase's exit functions before the new one's enter functions, and the tick's remaining rules run in the old phase. Going to the phase the scene is in leaves and enters it. `lasts(d).then(p)` changes phase at the tick `d` after entry. `phase.time()` is the time since entry. (4) A tick makes one transition at most, and the first request stands whichever kind it is. In each of these four pairs, made in this order in one tick, the first lands, the second returns false and nothing of the second happens: two `scenes.go_to`; two `PhaseMut::go_to`; a `PhaseMut::go_to` then a `scenes.go_to`; a `scenes.go_to` then a `PhaseMut::go_to`. In the tick a `lasts` runs out, a rule's `PhaseMut::go_to` to another phase lands and the `lasts` does not. (5) A request made while a transition lands. A `scenes.go_to` made by a phase's enter function, and one made by an exit function of a scene or of a phase, is the next tick's first request: that tick's rules run once, a rule's own request in it returns false, and the held one lands when that tick ends. A `PhaseMut::go_to` is held the same way where its scene is the one running once the landing ends: made by an enter function of the scene being entered, and by a phase's exit function during a change of phase. Made by an exit function of a scene that is being left, both for another scene that has no phases and by a `restart`, it returns false and no phase changes, and in the next tick a rule's `scenes.go_to` returns true and lands. (6) A scene given to `Game::scene` as a tuple of functions, or built with `scene.add`, is one scene whose entries run in the order those functions wrote them. (7) `Timer`: `running` is true from `start` until the tick its wait ends and `finished` from then on; both are false for `Timer::IDLE` and after `clear`. `Cooldown::take` is true at once from `Cooldown::READY`, then once in each `every`, and a changed `every` applies from the next take. (8) All of the above give the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

A scripted run of a test game that spawns, despawns, writes components and resources, changes phase and scene and draws from `Random`: (1) gives one world digest at every tick when run twice, when rewound to a tick inside the run and replayed, and when the same game is built again from its scene functions; (2) has a digest that covers the whole world: changing one field of one component, changing one field of one resource, spawning one entity, despawning one entity, and being in another phase or another scene each give another digest; (3) `Random` gives the same draws for the same seed, tick and rule, and other draws for another seed or another rule; (4) a rule that returns an error refuses its tick, in a tick where earlier rules had already written a component, written a resource, spawned an entity that a later rule then visited, and despawned one: afterwards every component value, resource value and entity count read back through the harness is what it was before the tick, the error names the rule and the tick, and the next `step()` runs as if the refused tick had not been tried; (5) on the Mac, a rule that panics is reported the same way, with the same values read back. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step, and leaves the world unchanged where a world exists. At compile time: a component, a resource, an event or a scene's field that is a `Vec`, a `String`, a reference, a raw float or `usize`; a first scene whose type has no default. At startup, as the error `test()` returns, with no tick stepped: a rule that reads a resource nothing provides; a rule with one `Query` that names a component twice, once with `&mut`, as `Query<(&mut Health, &Health)>` does, in a game with no entity, whose message names the rule, the parameter and the component. While running, each refusing its tick: a spawn of a component that no signature names and the game has not declared, whose message names the rule, the component and `Game::component`; an entity that two parameters of one rule both match on a component one of them writes, in each of three cases (both parameters write it; one writes it and the other reads it; an entity that matched one of them comes to match both when an earlier rule inserts a component), whose message names the rule, both parameters, the component and the entity; `Single` with none and with two; `go_to` a scene the game was not given; a spawn past the world's size; a rule that returns an error. Two parameters of one rule that name the same component, both writing it and one writing it while the other reads it, where no entity matches both, start and step with no complaint and no `Without`. A game whose scenes have no camera, no binding and no frame function starts and steps with no complaint. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

No public item of `thrum` names a type of `wgpu`, `winit` or another engine crate by that crate's path. Every public item of `thrum` has a doc comment with an example, and every example runs as a doc test. A package that names `thrum` with default features off builds alone and has no renderer, window, GPU, network or platform crate in its dependency closure. `thrum` and any crate it is built from are registered in `.config/architecture.toml`. Guard: the surface check and the doc tests run in `./dev check` from this landing, so every later work package's additions are held to them.
items.check: python3 scripts/sdk_surface.py check && cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --doc

items.statement: The SDK is a layer over the engine's simulation and adds no second one.
items.ask: Read `thrum` and the tests' games. 1. Is world state held anywhere but `thrum-core`'s registered simulation: is there a second store, clock or undo? Which scene and phase run are world state there too? 2. Are a rule's structural edits applied when the rule ends inside the tick's one transaction, so that a refused tick undoes them with everything else, and does a rule that staged none pay nothing for the barrier? 3. Is the loop over entities inside a rule monomorphised for that rule's parameters, with no dynamic call and no allocation for each entity, and no allocation for each tick once warm? One call for each rule each tick through the engine's registered callback is as designed. 4. Does a component's schema identity come from its name and fields, and never from a Rust type ID? 5. Are the changes made in `thrum-core` additions only, with its existing tests unedited and passing? 6. Does any test's game name a crate other than `thrum`, or a schema number, permit, executor, page or device?

items.statement: Game code for the headless subset is written as the design's worked examples write it. Every difference between the built API and the parts of the examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists is a line in the module's log, and none is a change of shape as the design's section "What a builder may change" defines one.
items.ask: Set the tests' games beside the parts of the worked examples that the design's section "What WP1 compiles" lists: from example A, `Score`, `drop_rocks` with its cadence, `fall`, and `Play` and `GameOver` joined by `go_to` with the score as the scene's field; from example E, `Run`, `Stage`, its three phase blocks with their lengths, `next_wave`, `enemies_die`, `heroes_fall` and `clear_enemies`. Set the rule parameters beside these rows of mechanism 3's table: `Query`, `Single`, `Res` and `ResMut`, `Entities`, `Events` and `Emit`, `Tick`, `Random`, `Scenes`, `Phase` and `PhaseMut`. Leave out what that section gives to later work packages. List each difference in how a game maker writes the same thing. Is each one in the log as a spelling? Is any a change of shape? A change of shape that is not the owner's own fails this item.

work_packages.name: A game names a reusable thing, spawns it and variants of it, attaches one thing to another and takes a thing out of play
work_packages.quality_bar: Reuse as plain as Unity's prefab variants and Godot's scenes, in Rust with no editor: a variant is a base and a difference, and a child is one line. The reference for how game code reads is the design's worked examples E and G, which the owner approves.

items.statement: Prefabs, in a game with no window started with `test()` and stepped. (1) A prefab named in a `prefabs!` block and defined with `Game::prefab` is spawned at a place with `.at` and `.at_point`, with the components of its definition. (2) `.with(c)` on a definition and on a spawn replaces the component of that type or adds it, and `.tweak` changes one field and leaves the others. (3) A variant is its base with its changes: every component the variant did not change has the base's value, and that still holds when the base is defined after the variant. (4) A `Prefab<N>` is spawned with the `N` its spawn brings. (5) A child and a named part given in a definition are spawned with the entity, at their local places, and despawned with it. (6) A prefab's components are known to the world with no other line. (7) A test spawns a prefab with `game.spawn` and gets its entity. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Children, parts and disabling, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. In (1) and (2) every number composes exactly: parents and children stand at whole-number positions, and parents are turned by quarter turns and scaled by two. (1) `attach(child).to(parent)` with `keep_world` leaves the child's place in the world bit for bit as it was, and with `keep_local(pose)` puts it at that local place. `detach` with `keep_world` leaves it bit for bit where it stood. (2) `world2d` and `world3d` give a child's place through two levels of such parents. (3) `parent` and `children` answer, the children in the order they were attached, and `part` reaches a named part. (4) Despawning a parent despawns its children and theirs. (5) Attaching, detaching and disabling land when the rule ends, as a spawn does. (6) A disabled entity and its children are visited by no query until enabled, keep their components, and are visited again from the rule after `enable`. (7) A child at x = 1/10, made by dividing one by ten, attached with `keep_world` under a parent at x = 10 scaled by two, a place no local transform recomposes bit for bit, is attached and not refused, and stands within one part in 2^17 of ten units of where it stood. (8) All of it gives the same world after a rewind and a replay, and the digest changes when a parent changes. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step. At compile time: a spawn of a `Prefab<N>` that does not bring its `N`. At startup, as the error `test()` returns, with no tick stepped: a name declared in a `prefabs!` block that has no definition, in each of four cases (only a rule's body spawns it, in a branch a run would first reach at its hundredth tick, from a block another of whose names the game defines; the same from a block of its own, none of whose names the game's description defines or names; a definition uses it as a base; a definition uses it as a child or a part), whose message names the prefab, its block and `Game::prefab`; a prefab that two parameters of one rule both match on a component one of them writes, whose message names the rule, the parameters, the component and the prefab. While running, each refusing its tick with the world unchanged: `part` on an entity whose prefab has no such part; an attachment that would make a cycle; `keep_world` under a parent whose scale is zero and under one whose scale is below 1/10,000, after each of which the child's parent, local place and place in the world read back as they were. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.
Prefabs and the tree cost nothing where they are not used, `keep_world` is held to its bound on every call, and both read as the design's examples do.
items.ask: 1. Is a prefab, with its variants, resolved once when the game starts, so that a spawn copies a prepared set of components with no lookup by name and no allocation? 2. Does an entity with no parent and no child hold or pay for anything of the tree, in a query and in the digest's work? 3. Is the place a `keep_world` recomposes compared with where the child stood on every call, and the attachment refused past the design's bound, with the residual and the bound in the error? 4. Set the tests' games beside example E's `prefabs` function, its spawns of `BAT`, `ELITE_BAT`, `GEM` and `SHOT`, and example G's `take_or_set_down`. Is each difference in the log as a spelling, and is none a change of shape as the design's section "What a builder may change" defines one?

work_packages.name: A crowd of 10,000 written on the SDK, steered by four players, steps identically on the Mac, in Chrome and on the iPhone simulator, and costs what the hand-written crowd does
work_packages.quality_bar: Determinism as Factorio holds it: the same inputs give the same world on every machine, checked by digest. Speed as the engine's own reference crowd: the layer is not what a tick is spent on. A first character that is steered as directly as Godot's first-game player. Rules that read as example E of the design does.

items.statement:
Players, action maps and a controlled character, in a game started with `test()` and stepped. Action maps: a rule reads a player's map with `Inputs::of` as plain fields, and an `Axis` and a `Stick` multiply and compare as a `Num` and a `Vec2`. Buttons: `held` is true while the button is down; `pressed` is true in exactly one tick for a press, the first admitted after it; `released` is true in the tick the button is found up after being held; `presses` is how many times it went down since the last tick. With a player's frames lost through the harness: a frame repeated for a missing one gives no press and keeps what was held; a neutral frame releases what was held; frames that come back after a neutral one give no press when no press was made in the gap, and one press, read in one tick, when one was; two presses between two admitted frames give `presses == 2` in one tick. Players: `PlayerJoined` is read once for a player, at the tick they enter the game, and not again in a later scene; `PlayerLeft`, `PlayerAway` and `PlayerBack` are read at the tick of each; `Players` gives who is here in seat order, the host and each player's status, and has no method that changes the roster; a game stepped with no roster script has one player from the first tick. A `scene.players().spawn(..).control(..)` line: gives a character to each player already here when the scene is entered and to each who arrives later, so that with two players joined in a first scene, a second scene with such a line has two characters, a third player who joins later makes three, and no player ever has two; a spawn function is given `Joined` and read-only parameters; a character is despawned when its player leaves, stays under idle input while they are away, and follows `when_away` when that says otherwise; `PlayersMut::respawn` brings back one a rule despawned. The control function runs where its line is written among the scene's entries, once a tick for each player's character in seat order, with that character's components and that player's map, so two players steering different ways each move their own; `.during(phase)` runs it only in that phase; alone it may also take `Res`, `Phase

` and `Emit`, and an event it sends is read by later rules of the tick. Seats and bots: a person who joins takes the lowest free seat; `PlayersMut::add_bot` takes the highest free seat, is announced as a player is and returns none when every seat is taken; input a rule sets with `BotInputs` before the control line is read by the control function in the same tick; a bot's character is spawned, moved and despawned as a person's is; a person who joins when bots hold every free seat takes the lowest seat a bot holds, and in that tick `PlayerLeft` is read for the bot, its character is despawned, `PlayerJoined` is read for the person, the person has one new character and no seat has two; a person who joins when people hold every seat is refused, the harness's `join()` returning the full error with no event read, no character spawned and no seat changed. All of it gives the same world after a rewind to a tick inside the run and a replay. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

`Space2d` over entities with a `Collider2d`. (1) `touching`, `within`, `in_rect`, `nearest` and `sweep_circle` find the same set of entities `thrum-sim2d`'s queries find for the same circles, and exactly the overlapping ones for rectangles and capsules, with offsets, on the layer asked, less any entity named by `except`. The order they come in is the SDK's own, whatever order the index gives: nearest first with ties by spawn order, and for `sweep_circle` earliest contact first with ties by spawn order. (2) `.on(LAYER)` answers from that layer's colliders alone: `nearest` on one layer returns that layer's nearest collider when colliders of another layer stand nearer, with a radius and without one. A query with no `.on` returns every layer's answer merged in the same order. (3) A query answers from where colliders are when its rule starts: it finds an entity the previous rule spawned or moved where it now is, and does not find one the previous rule despawned. `at_tick_start()` answers from where colliders stood when the tick began. (4) `motion_of(entity).sweep()` reports the earliest contact along the path the entity took this tick against the paths the others took: a body moved through another between two ticks is reported hit, one spawned this tick is swept from where it was spawned, and a tie goes to the earlier spawned. (5) A layer's index is built at most once after each rule that changed that layer and not at all in a tick that changed none, which a count the test reads shows. (6) A scene's cell size is part of its rule set. Guard: CPU tests on small worlds, in `./dev check`.

The numbers page holds, the profile's additions are exactly rounded and refuse what a rule may not reach, and nothing retained changed. Every row of the table in the design's mechanism 9 marked allowed compiles and gives the value written, and each row marked not allowed fails to compile or is refused by the check, as that row says. An integer converts as that table says: 16,777,216 exactly, and 16,777,217 to 16,777,216. `num`, `Vec2::lit` and `Seconds::lit` are usable in a `const`. `Angle` and its `sin`, `cos` and directions, turning a `Vec2` and a `Vec3`, and `Rot3` products have conformance vectors beside the profile's own. A child attached with `keep_world` under a parent turned by 37 degrees and scaled by 1.5, within 100 units of the origin, stands within 0.001 of a unit of where it stood. The profile's controls refuse, each with a message that names the reason, checked rules that read a file through `std::fs`, open a socket through `std::net`, start a process through `std::process` or read standard input, beside every refusal the profile already made. The reference crowd's retained digests are unchanged. Guard: the vectors, the profile check and its controls run in `./dev check`.
items.check: cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum --test it numbers:: && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py check && python3 scripts/sim2d_profile.py controls && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-2d --test retained_slice

items.statement: Each of these mistakes is refused with a message that carries its stable code and names the object, the cause and the next step. At compile time: a field of an action map with neither `#[bind]` nor `#[sent]`; a `LocalActions` map asked for by a rule; a field of world state that is a raw float, whose message names `Num`; a spawn function given to `players().spawn` that takes `PlayersMut`, `ResMut<T>` or `Entities`. At startup, as the error `test()` returns: action maps that do not fit an input frame, with the counts and the limit; a control function that takes `&mut T` and `&T` of one component of its character; a control function with a `Query` that reaches the character its line spawns, over a component either writes. While running, each refusing its tick with the world unchanged: two characters for one player on one `players()` line; a player's character that comes to be reached by a `Query` of its own control function over a component either writes, in each of two cases (a rule inserts a component on the character; `PlayersMut::possess` gives the player an entity the query matches, after which the player's character reads back as the one it was), whose message names the function, the parameter, the component, the player and the entity. A control function that takes `&mut Transform2d` for its character beside a `Query<&Transform2d, With<Enemy>>` starts and steps with no complaint and no `Without`, and still does after `possess` gives the player another entity that is no enemy, which the function then moves. The tests hold each message's code, object, cause and next step by its text. Guard: in `./dev check`.

On the Mac, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, and its trace row carries these witnesses, each more than nothing: for each of the four players, how far their hero moved along the direction that player's script steers, the four scripts steering up, down, left and right; hits; deaths; respawns; the angle the turning body turned through; how many prefab names the SDK knew when the game started, before it read the game's description, which is every name `crowd-sdk` declares; and ticks a rule refused by returning an error at a scripted tick, after each of which the components and resources read back were what they were before it. `crowd-sdk` is a game under `examples/crowd-sdk` that names only `thrum`, with its rules in its `rules` module: four players' heroes moved by a control function on a `scene.players()` line, enemies that chase the nearest hero and keep apart with `par_each`, shots at the nearest enemy that hit by `motion_of(..).sweep()`, deaths that drop a pick-up collected in the same tick, respawns, and a body that turns by an `Angle` each tick, at 10,000 bodies. Record: the Mac arm of the three-target conformance run. A slice of the trace, with its witnesses, stays as a CPU test in `./dev check`.
items.check: python3 scripts/sim2d_conformance.py run --package crowd-sdk --target mac-metal && cargo test --locked --offline -p crowd-sdk --test it retained::

items.statement: In Chrome, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. The conformance runner takes Chrome's lock itself around its browser run, so the item names none. Record: the Chrome arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the iPhone simulator, `crowd-sdk` gives the digests its retained trace holds, with every witness WP2.5 names more than nothing. Function only. The conformance runner takes the simulator for each of its turns itself, so the item names no lock. Record: the simulator arm of the three-target conformance run.

On the Mac, two release takes each of `crowd-sdk` and of the reference crowd at 10,000 bodies report the cost of a tick, of a rewind and of a replay, and the allocations of a warmed tick, side by side, with the build and the load on the machine. The takes of `crowd-sdk` are of the load WP2.5 describes: the record carries, counted over the measured ticks, each of the four players' hero movement, hits, deaths and respawns, each more than nothing, and how many times each layer's index was built in a tick, beside the reference's own witnesses for its takes. The record flags for investigation a `crowd-sdk` tick more than about 25% above the reference's, and any allocation in a warmed `crowd-sdk` tick. The check fails only on a missing measurement or a missing witness. The record also names the default number of entities a world holds and why. Record: SDK rule cost beside the hand-written reference, taken under load.
`crowd-sdk` reads as example E of the design does, and what the SDK added to the engine for it belongs to the engine's owners.
items.ask: 1. Read `crowd-sdk`'s rules beside example E. Does its scene function read top to bottom as one tick, and does each rule read as one thing the game does? Does the package hold a helper file that hides plumbing a game maker would have to write: registration, encoding, scheduling, index building? Count every file of the package as game lines. 2. Is each difference from the design's examples in the log as a spelling, and is none a change of shape? 3. Are the profile's additions in `thrum-core`'s profile and `thrum-sim2d`, with no platform maths call, and do the reference crowd's rules and retained traces stand unedited? 4. Does `Space2d` keep one `thrum-sim2d` index for each layer with its storage between ticks, and answer a query on a layer from that layer's index alone, so that an enemy's nearest-hero query looks at the heroes and not at the crowd? 5. Is the heroes' control function their whole movement step, writing the pose itself?

items.statement: A game outside the engine checkout, one package laid out as the design's templates are with its rules in `src/rules.rs` and reaching the engine by path, passes the engine's external game check and the check of its own rules, and its own test starts it with `test()`. The same game fails its own check, with a message that names the line and the violation, with each of these in its `rules` module: raw-float arithmetic; a file read; a call to a function defined elsewhere in the game. It still passes with float arithmetic in a frame function outside that module. The same game is refused at startup, as the error `test()` returns, with a message that names the function and the `rules` module, with each of these defined outside that module: a rule; a control function; a spawn function given to `scene.players().spawn(..)`; an enter function; a condition. A game that keeps its rules in a package of its own, marked in that package's manifest, passes the same way and fails the same way. The engine's check of its registered rule packages still passes throughout, and the external game check still refuses a game package that names an engine example and a path that leaves the game's folder for anything but the engine's crates. Guard: a test over scratch games outside the checkout, in `./dev check`.
